story: XPRIZE Wildfire awards $4.55M on September 23rd, with the Autonomous Wildfire Response track decided by June finals testing at Nenana, Alaska

claims.claim: XPRIZE announced the XPRIZE Wildfire awardees on September 23rd at a ceremony held at the New York City Fire Museum.
claims.verbatim: The awardees were announced during the XPRIZE Wildfire Awards Ceremony held at the New York City Fire Museum.
claims.notes: The dateline reads 'NEW YORK, Sept. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/' and it was released at 12:00 ET. The xprize.org awardees page confirms the ceremony at the New York City Fire Museum. This is XPRIZE's own release, so it is primary.

claims.claim: XPRIZE Wildfire awarded a total of $4.55 million across both of its tracks.
claims.verbatim: XPRIZE Wildfire Awards $4.55M to Innovators Advancing Wildfire Detection and Response
claims.notes: This is the release headline. The body gives no $4.55 million figure. The sum reconciles, since $3.5M for Track B (including the $1M Lockheed Martin bonus) plus $1.05M for Track A equals $4.55M. That figure does NOT match the xprize.org page's $2.5M Track B figure plus $1.05M. See S1-C05.

claims.claim: XPRIZE Wildfire is an $11 million global competition that launched in 2023.
claims.verbatim: an $11 million global competition launched in 2023 to accelerate innovation in firefighting technologies
claims.notes: The xprize.org awardees page corroborates it ('the $11 million XPRIZE Wildfire Competition'), as does the January finalists page title ('$11M Competition'). $11M is the size of the competition, and only $4.55M was awarded on September 23rd. The deck must not suggest $11M was paid out.

claims.claim: According to the XPRIZE release on PR Newswire, the judging panel awarded $3.5 million across the three Autonomous Wildfire Response finalist teams.
claims.verbatim: The XPRIZE Wildfire Judging Panel awarded $3.5 million across three Track B Finalist teams
claims.notes: RECONCILIATION. The place awards are $1.2M + $800,000 + $500,000 = $2.5M. The $3.5M figure only works if you add the $1M Lockheed Martin bonus, which also went to a Track B team (Anduril). So $3.5M INCLUDES the bonus and $2.5M EXCLUDES it. Suggested hedge: 'Track B awards totaled $2.5 million, or $3.5 million with the Lockheed Martin bonus.'

claims.claim: The XPRIZE awardees page and Dryad's release both give $2.5 million for the three Track B finalist teams, a figure that excludes the $1 million Lockheed Martin bonus.
claims.verbatim: The XPRIZE Wildfire Judging Panel awarded $2.5 million across three Track B Finalist teams
claims.notes: The identical sentence appears in Dryad's Business Wire release, with $2.5 million. The xprize.org page carries no date stamp and says 'Today, XPRIZE announced'. The date is taken from the PR Newswire release. That the figure excludes the bonus is arithmetic (1.2 + 0.8 + 0.5 = 2.5), and the bonus is listed separately on the same page.

claims.claim: XPRIZE awarded $1.05 million across five teams in Track A, the space-based wildfire detection track.
claims.verbatim: XPRIZE awarded $1.05 million across five Track A teams, recognizing meaningful advances in space-based wildfire detection and intelligence.
claims.notes: The Track A line items reconcile to $1.05M: SIRIUS Wildfire Alliance $500,000, Team Snuffed $250,000, and $100,000 each to MyRadar, DeepFire and Mayday.AI. The xprize.org awardees page lists the same five.

claims.claim: SIRIUS Wildfire Alliance won first place in Track A, the space-based detection track, and $500,000.
claims.verbatim: $500,000: SIRIUS Wildfire Alliance
claims.notes: It is listed as 'First Place - System Integration Awardee'. The verbatim is cut to leave out a dash character whose exact glyph was not confirmed. Second place went to Team Snuffed ($250,000). The PR Newswire release corroborates it. Track A testing was in Australia, not Alaska (S1-C33).

claims.claim: Anduril Industries won first place in the Autonomous Wildfire Response track and $1.2 million.
claims.verbatim: First Place Awardee, $1.2 Million: Anduril Industries
claims.notes: The identical line appears on xprize.org/news/xprize-wildfire-awardees.

claims.claim: Dryad Networks won second place in the Autonomous Wildfire Response track and $800,000.
claims.verbatim: Second Place Awardee, $800,000: Dryad Networks
claims.notes: Corroborated by xprize.org and by Dryad's own release ('announced it has been awarded $800,000 in the XPRIZE Wildfire competition for its performance in the Autonomous Wildfire Response finals in Alaska').

claims.claim: AURA Foresight won third place in the Autonomous Wildfire Response track and $500,000.
claims.verbatim: Third Place Awardee, $500,000: AURA Foresight
claims.notes: The identical line appears on xprize.org.

claims.claim: Anduril Industries also won the $1 million Lockheed Martin Accurate Detection Intelligence Bonus Prize for its multi-sensor detector performance.
claims.verbatim: The Lockheed Martin Accurate Detection Intelligence Bonus Prize of $1 million was awarded to Anduril Industries for their rapid and precise multi-sensor detector performance.
claims.notes: xprize.org names it 'Lockheed Martin Accurate Detection & Intelligence Bonus Prize, $1,000,000: Anduril Industries' (with an ampersand). Anduril's combined $2.2M is ARITHMETIC and appears on no page. If the deck uses it, write it as a sum of the two named awards.

claims.claim: Track B teams were challenged to autonomously detect and completely suppress a high-risk fire within 10 minutes of ignition.
claims.verbatim: Teams were challenged to autonomously detect and completely suppress a high-risk fire within 10 minutes of ignition across 1,000 km² of challenging terrain, without disturbing nearby decoy fires.
claims.notes: The same wording appears on the xprize.org awardees page, and Dryad's release has a near-identical version. This states the CHALLENGE and is not a result.

claims.claim: The Track B test area covered 1,000 square kilometers of challenging terrain.
claims.verbatim: across 1,000 km² of challenging terrain
claims.notes: The January finalists page corroborates it ('a 1,000 km² test zone'). 1,000 km2 is about 386 square miles, a unit conversion that no page states.

claims.claim: Track B systems had to suppress the target fire without disturbing nearby decoy fires.
claims.verbatim: without disturbing nearby decoy fires
claims.notes: Also in PR Newswire. The finals-testing page says AURA used a DJI Mavic 'to distinguish active fires from decoys'.

claims.claim: Autonomous Wildfire Response competitors tested their systems in the Alaskan wilderness in June 2026.
claims.verbatim: In June 2026, Autonomous Wildfire Response competitors put their solutions to the test in the Alaskan wilderness.
claims.notes: The same sentence is on xprize.org. The September 23rd release does not name Nenana. Nenana comes from the July 1st finals-testing page (S1-C16).

claims.claim: Over two weeks in June 2026, finalist teams deployed autonomous systems in rural Nenana, Alaska, in partnership with the University of Alaska Fairbanks.
claims.verbatim: Over two weeks in June 2026, finalist teams deployed autonomous systems in rural Nenana, Alaska, just outside of Fairbanks, in partnership with the University of Alaska Fairbanks.
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. The page is dated July 1st, outside the window. It is a live blog with entries dated June 11th to June 30th. Note that 'just outside of Fairbanks' is XPRIZE's wording, and Nenana is roughly 55 road miles from Fairbanks. Keep it attributed or drop that phrase.

claims.claim: The finals testing site was at the Nenana Municipal Airport, where ACUASI performs flight operations and managed the surrounding airspace during the competition.
claims.verbatim: the Finals Testing site was situated at the Nenana Municipal Airport, where the Alaska Center for Unmanned Aircraft Systems Integration (ACUASI), performs flight operations and whose team safely managed the surrounding airspace throughout the competition.
claims.notes: BACKGROUND (July 1st page). Returned identically in two separate fetches. The same page credits ACUASI's partnership with making 'autonomous flight operations possible throughout the competition'. Dedupe context: UAF News of September 16th reports a separate ACUASI blood-sample drone flight from the same airport (No.62), a different story.

claims.claim: Official finals testing at Nenana was scheduled to begin on June 15th.
claims.verbatim: Official testing is set to commence on June 15.
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. It comes from the live-blog entry dated June 11th. It is a SCHEDULE statement, and no page confirms that testing actually began that day. Hedge it as 'scheduled to begin June 15th'. The team-profile entries are dated June 27th, 29th and 30th.

claims.claim: The Nenana test site lay along the Nenana-Totchaket Road corridor.
claims.verbatim: The testing site, located along the Nenana-Totchaket Road corridor, provided a large, sparsely developed landscape
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. Useful for a map, since the Totchaket corridor runs west across the Tanana River from Nenana.

claims.claim: At Nenana, each team had to monitor a vast area for 8 hours and detect, locate and suppress up to three controlled incipient-stage wildfires without human intervention.
claims.verbatim: teams are being challenged to monitor a vast area for 8 hours and rapidly detect, locate, and suppress up to three controlled incipient stage wildfires without human intervention.
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. 'Controlled' fires means they were set on purpose. No page gives the size of the fires, how they were lit, or how many were actually set per team. The site fetch explicitly reports that none of this is stated.

claims.claim: Three finalists competed in the June 2026 Alaska finals.
claims.verbatim: In June 2026, three finalists were challenged to autonomously detect and completely suppress a high-risk wildfire within 10 minutes of ignition across 1,000 km² of Alaskan wilderness, leaving any decoy fires untouched.
claims.notes: The XPRIZE release corroborates it ('three Track B Finalist teams'). The finals-testing page names them as Anduril, AURA Foresight and DRYAD. Hosted on a FinancialContent mirror of Business Wire. This is the company's own statement, so it is primary.

claims.claim: AURA Foresight rejoined the competition after a finalist spot opened, combining two former semifinalist teams from the UK and Australia.
claims.verbatim: AURA Foresight has rejoined the competition following a finalist spot opening, bringing together two former semifinalist teams from the UK and Australia under one name.
claims.notes: BACKGROUND (live-blog entry of June 29th). This explains why AURA is missing from January's five finalists (S1-C23). The pages do NOT say why Data Blanket, FireSwarm Solutions and Wildfire Quest did not compete in the finals. Do not infer a reason.

claims.claim: In January, XPRIZE named five Autonomous Wildfire Response finalists, Anduril, Data Blanket, Dryad, FireSwarm Solutions and Wildfire Quest.
claims.verbatim: Five Finalist teams are: Anduril (USA), Data Blanket (USA), Dryad (Germany), FireSwarm Solutions (Canada), and Wildfire Quest (USA)
claims.notes: BACKGROUND (January 29th, out of window). The scout's '3 finalists' is correct for the June finals only. Five finalists were named in January and three competed in June.

claims.claim: XPRIZE awarded $750,000 across the autonomous finalist teams when it announced them in January.
claims.verbatim: $750,000 Awarded Across Autonomous Teams to Advance their Drone and AI Coordination Solutions
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. This is the page subheadline. The fetches disagreed on capitalization ('Advance' against 'advance'). It is a milestone award, separate from the $4.55M announced September 23rd.

claims.claim: XPRIZE field-tested 13 Autonomous Semifinalist teams in late 2025.
claims.verbatim: In late 2025, the XPRIZE Wildfire operations team conducted in-field testing with 13 Autonomous Semifinalist teams
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. It supports the funnel of about 300 entrants to 13 semifinalists to 5 finalists to 3 at the finals.

claims.claim: According to Dryad, it advanced from an original field of approximately 300 entrants in the four-year competition.
claims.verbatim: Dryad advanced from an original field of approximately 300 entrants in the four-year competition.
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. This is Dryad's figure, and no XPRIZE page fetched here states an entrant count. Attribute it: 'about 300 entrants, according to Dryad'. It is unclear whether 300 covers both tracks. 'Four-year' is consistent with a 2023 launch.

claims.claim: Dryad's Silvanet is a 170-sensor persistent field network, which XPRIZE credited with Silvaguard drones for demonstrating end-to-end autonomy.
claims.verbatim: Dryad's Silvanet, a 170-sensor persistent field network, combined with their Silvaguard drones, demonstrated end-to-end autonomy.
claims.notes: Dryad's release corroborates it ('Dryad's 170-sensor persistent Silvanet field network combined with Silvaguard drones for demonstrating end-to-end autonomy').

claims.claim: According to Dryad, its Silvanet network detected and verified the target fire in 12 minutes or less and autonomously launched a response.
claims.verbatim: During the tests, the Dryad's Silvanet sensor network successfully detected and verified target fire in 12 minutes or less and autonomously launched a response, ignoring any decoy fires.
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. This is the company's own claim, and XPRIZE does not state it. SANITY CHECK: 12 minutes is LONGER than the 10-minute target, and it covers detection and verification only, not suppression. The deck must not present it as meeting the 10-minute goal.

claims.claim: Dryad's Suppression Drone deploys up to 100 liters of suppressant on a fire.
claims.verbatim: A Suppression Drone then deploys up to 100 liters of suppressant on the fire.
claims.notes: This is a product capability stated by the company. The release does not say how much was deployed in the Alaska test. 100 liters is about 26 US gallons, a conversion no page states.

claims.claim: According to Dryad, its Suppression Drone accurately hit the fire with suppressant during the Alaska tests.
claims.verbatim: the Suppression Drone accurately hit the fire with suppressant
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. This is a company claim. The full sentence continues by calling it 'a strong proof of concept for the competition end goal', which implicitly concedes that the end goal was not reached. The release does NOT say the fire was fully suppressed.

claims.claim: XPRIZE said AURA Foresight met the critical 10-minute detection gate with autonomous and persistent detection.
claims.verbatim: AURA successfully demonstrated autonomous and persistent detection, meeting the critical 10-minute detection gate.
claims.notes: This is the only explicit statement in any source that a team met a 10-minute gate, and it concerns DETECTION, not suppression.

claims.claim: XPRIZE credited Anduril's Lattice software platform with an integrated detection-to-suppression pathway unifying cameras, sensors and drones.
claims.verbatim: Anduril's modular Lattice software platform provided an integrated detection-to-suppression integrated pathway for unifying cameras, sensors and drones.
claims.notes: The doubled 'integrated' is in the original. The finals-testing blog (June 27th) calls the platform 'Lattice Fire' and says it pairs Sentry Tower sensing with Ghost-X aircraft. The payload detail was not captured verbatim (see killed).

claims.claim: Track A testing for space-based detection concluded in New South Wales, Australia, in April.
claims.verbatim: Testing for Track A, Space-Based Detection & Intelligence, concluded in New South Wales, Australia, in April.
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. It makes clear that only Track B was decided in Alaska. The Minderoo quote in the September 23rd release corroborates it ('alongside the NSW Rural Fire Service').

claims.claim: The September 23rd XPRIZE release does not state whether any team fully suppressed a fire within 10 minutes, and Lockheed Martin's Adam Broecker said the final prize remains on the horizon.
claims.verbatim: While the final prize remains on the horizon, every milestone achieved in this competition brings us closer to giving firefighters, communities, and mutual aid networks the transformative tools they need to stay ahead of the fire.
claims.notes: This is a CLAIM ABOUT THE RECORD. None of the five fetched pages states that any team detected AND fully suppressed a fire within 10 minutes. XPRIZE uses 'awardee' and 'breakthroughs', not 'winner of the grand prize'. The Broecker quote is by Adam Broecker, Vice President, LM Evolve, Lockheed Martin. Do NOT write 'the grand prize went unclaimed', because no page says it. Suggested wording: 'XPRIZE's announcement does not say any team met the full 10-minute suppression target.'

claims.claim: XPRIZE Wildfire program director Andrea Santy said the teams helped identify where continued innovation is needed before real-world deployment at scale.
claims.verbatim: These teams pushed the boundaries of what is possible today, demonstrating meaningful advances in wildfire detection and response while helping identify where continued innovation is needed to move these technologies toward real-world deployment at scale.
claims.notes: It is attributed to 'Andrea Santy, XPRIZE Wildfire Executive Program Director'. Her title on the January page is 'XPRIZE Wildfire Program Director'. Use the September title.

claims.claim: Dryad CEO Carsten Brinkschulte said drones can suppress a small ignition but their limited payload makes them largely ineffective once a wildfire has grown out of control.
claims.verbatim: Drones can suppress a small ignition, but their limited payload makes them largely ineffective once a wildfire has grown out of control.
claims.notes: This is part of a longer quote from 'Carsten Brinkschulte, CEO and Co-Founder of Dryad Networks'. The same quote includes 'Our vision is fully aligned with XPRIZE Wildfire: detect and extinguish fires within 10 minutes of ignition.'

claims.claim: XPRIZE says Alaska's 2025 wildfire season burned an estimated 1.68 million acres.
claims.verbatim: In 2025 alone, Alaska experienced a wildfire season that burned an estimated 1.68 million acres.
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. XPRIZE is primary for its own competition but SECONDARY for Alaska fire statistics. The authoritative source would be the Alaska Interagency Coordination Center, which was not fetched this run. Attribute it: 'an estimated 1.68 million acres, according to XPRIZE'. Taken from the 'Why Alaska?' entry dated June 18th (background).

claims.claim: XPRIZE describes Interior Alaska testing conditions as unpredictable weather, long distances, rugged terrain and abundant wildlife.
claims.verbatim: Teams must contend with unpredictable weather, long distances, rugged terrain, and abundant wildlife.
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. This is a general description. No page reports the actual weather on test days.

claims.claim: The VIP Day at the finals was welcomed by UAF Vice Chancellor for Research Laura Conner and ACUASI Director Catherine Cahill.
claims.verbatim: Guests were welcomed by University of Alaska Fairbanks Vice Chancellor for Research Dr. Laura Conner and Dr. Catherine Cahill, Director of the Alaska Center for Unmanned Aircraft Systems Integration (ACUASI).
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. The only Alaska institutional roles named on any page are UAF (partner) and ACUASI (flight operations and airspace). No page names the Alaska Division of Forestry and Fire Protection, the Alaska Fire Service or the BLM. The judges are not named on the page and are linked to a separate Judges page that was not fetched.

claims.claim: Former U.S. Fire Administrator Lori Moore-Merrell called the finals VIP event a genuine inflection point in how humanity responds to wildfire.
claims.verbatim: a genuine inflection point in how humanity responds to wildfire
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. It is a quoted fragment reported by XPRIZE and not the full sentence. Use it only as a partial quote attributed 'as quoted by XPRIZE'.

claims.claim: XPRIZE Wildfire now moves into a 12- to 15-month Impact Phase aimed at turning the technologies into deployable wildfire tools.
claims.verbatim: The competition will now move into a 12- to 15-month Impact Phase focused on helping translate promising technologies from both tracks into durable, deployable solutions for real-world wildfire management.
claims.notes: xprize.org confirms the Impact Phase but gives no duration. PG&E's Mark Quinlan calls PG&E the 'Impact Phase Partner'. No page says anything about future testing or deployment in Alaska.

claims.claim: Dryad plans real-world operational pilots of its system in 2027 and targets commercial availability in 2028.
claims.verbatim: Dryad will now invest significantly in productizing Silvaguard, with real-world operational pilots planned for 2027 and commercial availability targeted for 2028.
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. This is a company projection. Use 'plans' or 'targets'. No location is given for the pilots.

claims.claim: XPRIZE Wildfire was sponsored by PG&E, the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, Minderoo Foundation and Lockheed Martin.
claims.verbatim: Sponsored by PG&E and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation as well as Minderoo Foundation and Lockheed Martin
claims.notes: No independent Alaska or trade outlet coverage of the September 23rd awards was found. UAF News lists nothing on XPRIZE (the September 16th ACUASI story is about blood transport). DroneLife's only XPRIZE item is dated May 18th, and the DuckDuckGo, Bing and Google searches were blocked or returned junk. Every Story 1 claim therefore rests on XPRIZE's and Dryad's own statements.

claims.claim: Governor candidate Dave Bronson said he is a big believer in data centers.
claims.verbatim: I'm a big believer in data centers. I know that might be unpopular with some folks here
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: It was said at a Commonwealth North forum. The Beacon original is dated September 18th, and both republications are in window. KTOO (September 22nd) has the identical words. There is one reported source, three republications. The apostrophe may be curly on the page.

claims.claim: Governor candidate Treg Taylor said of data centers that we need to embrace it.
claims.verbatim: I think we need to embrace it
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: Corroborated by the KTOO republication. The date of the forum could not be pinned consistently across fetches, so do not state it.

claims.claim: Governor candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins said he supports a moratorium on data center development in Alaska until the Legislature passes a comprehensive regulatory framework.
claims.verbatim: I support a moratorium on data center development in Alaska until the Legislature can pass a comprehensive regulatory framework
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: The verbatim is truncated to the portion confirmed in every fetch. Two fetches show it continuing 'for that development in Alaska.' One fetch and the scout end it at 'framework'. Quote only the confirmed portion. The KTOO prefix matches.

claims.claim: Governor candidate Bernadette Wilson said she will never allow Alaska to be littered with hyperscale data centers.
claims.verbatim: I will never allow Alaska to be littered with hyperscale data centers that take our resources and spoil our lands.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: The KTOO prefix matches. The scout's version was a shorter paraphrase.

claims.claim: The Alaska Senate passed CSSB 250(CRA) on reconsideration on May 16th by a vote of 14 to 5 with one excused.
claims.verbatim: PASSED ON RECONSIDERATION Y14 N5 E1
claims.notes: BACKGROUND date (May). The Senate Journal page is 2696. The first third-reading vote the same day was Y13 N5 E2 (p. 2690). The Beacon says it 'voted 14-5 to pass a data center bill', which is consistent. The record was read through the r.jina.ai proxy because akleg.gov returns 403 to bots.

claims.claim: SB 250 was referred to House Community and Regional Affairs on May 17th, heard and held on May 18th, and never taken up further before the session ended.
claims.verbatim: HCRA heard & held
claims.notes: The BASIS history ends at the May 18th HCRA entry ('recessed to call of chair'). The Beacon: 'the House did not consider it before the session concluded' (paraphrase-level fetch). The Beacon's framing and BASIS agree in substance, since there was a hearing but no committee action. Do not write that the House never heard it. The bill is not law.

claims.claim: Senator Loki Tobin introduced SB 250 on February 18th.
claims.verbatim: BY SENATOR TOBIN
claims.source_outlet: Alaska State Legislature, SB 250 introduced version
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. The header reads 'Introduced: 2/18/26'. BASIS reads '2/18/2026 ... Read first time; referred to CRA, L&C'. Alaska Public spells the name 'Loki Tobin' with an umlaut.

claims.claim: The Senate-passed CSSB 250(CRA) applies to data centers drawing 15 megawatts of peak power demand from an electric utility.
claims.verbatim: 15 megawatts of peak power demand from an electric utility
claims.source_outlet: Alaska State Legislature, CSSB 250(CRA) bill text
claims.notes: This is the proposed AS 42.05.435(l)(1). The gas threshold is '1,500,000,000 standard cubic feet of gas annually from a gas utility'. The introduced version used 20 MW or 20 percent of prior-year sales, and 2,000,000,000 scf. The date is when the committee moved the CS (April 21st). Background. The fetch paraphrased the surrounding sentence, so quote only the threshold phrase.

claims.claim: CSSB 250(CRA) would bar utilities from putting data center costs into rates unless those costs are recovered solely from the data center.
claims.verbatim: unless the rates or charges are designed to recover those costs solely from the data center
claims.source_outlet: Alaska State Legislature, CSSB 250(CRA) bill text
claims.notes: This is the proposed AS 42.05.381(r). The bill also requires the RCA to approve each contract, a municipal community benefit agreement before approval, and a decommissioning and recycling plan (proposed AS 46.03.125(a)). Describe it as what the bill 'would' do, because it did not pass.

claims.claim: The Pentagon has offered to lease about 4,700 acres of government land in Alaska to private companies for data centers.
claims.verbatim: It's offered to lease about 4,700 acres of government land to private companies, though no projects have been awarded yet.
claims.source_outlet: KUAC (Shelby Herbert), via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: WUNC American Homefront (September 22nd) has 'The Pentagon has offered to lease about 4,700 acres of government land in the state to private companies, though no projects have been awarded yet.' Air & Space Forces (April 11th, background) gives '4,700 acres located across Air Force and Space Force installations in Alaska'.

claims.claim: As of mid-September, no Alaska military data center projects had been awarded.
claims.verbatim: though no projects have been awarded yet
claims.notes: Two pieces by the same reporter (September 15th and 22nd), not independent. The primary solicitation record shows only that responses were due June 29th (S3-C05), with no award notice seen.

claims.claim: The Pentagon wants to build up to a dozen military data centers near Anchorage, Healy and Fairbanks.
claims.verbatim: The Pentagon wants to build up to a dozen new military data centers near Anchorage, Healy and Fairbanks.
claims.source_outlet: KUAC (Shelby Herbert), via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: Air & Space Forces (April 11th, background): 'Twelve parcels have been identified for potential development'. Twelve parcels is not the same as twelve data centers. The Air Force says 'potentially a dozen'. Hedge with 'up to'.

claims.claim: Senator Lisa Murkowski said she is not a proponent of data centers at JBER or Interior installations because of an insecure energy base.
claims.verbatim: I am not a proponent of data centers down at JBER or at our Interior installations because we are not able to support them because of an insecure energy base at this time,
claims.source_outlet: KUAC (Shelby Herbert), via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: Verbatim across two fetches, and WUNC September 22nd has the same words with a lowercase 'interior'. There is no primary Murkowski statement, so it is attributed as 'she said' to the KUAC reporting.

claims.claim: Air Force solicitation AFCEC-26-R-0006 sought AI data center developers at JBER, Eielson Air Force Base and Clear Space Force Station, with responses due June 29th after an extension from May 29th.
claims.verbatim: RFLP Artificial Intelligence (AI) Data Center Development at Joint Base Elmendorf Richardson, Eielson Air Force Base, and Clear Space Force Station
claims.notes: BACKGROUND (posted April 10th). This is an aggregator mirror of the SAM.gov notice. The SAM API records were not fetched this run, so it is marked non-primary. The due date shows 'June 29, 2026, 5:00 p.m. EDT (original: May 29, 2026...)'. The authority is 10 U.S.C. 2667, 'not less than the fair market value of the leasehold interest'.

claims.claim: At least 100 communities nationwide have adopted moratoria on building data centers.
claims.verbatim: At least 100 communities across the nation have adopted moratoria on building them, as opposition spreads from local jurisdictions to state legislatures.
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. It is a national tally with no underlying source given. Attribute it as 'according to American Homefront'. The same sentence appears in the September 15th Alaska Public piece.

stories_surviving: XPRIZE Wildfire awards $4.55M, Autonomous Wildfire Response track decided at Nenana, Alaska finals
Four Alaska governor candidates split on data centers as SB 250 stalls in House CRA
Air Force offers about 4,700 acres at Alaska bases for AI data centers, no award, Murkowski opposed

killed.claim: The XPRIZE Wildfire grand prize went unclaimed, or no team met the 10-minute suppression target.
killed.why: No fetched page states it. Only the absence of any such statement, plus Broecker's 'final prize remains on the horizon', is verifiable (see S1-C34). Stating an outcome would be inference.

killed.claim: Track B awards totaled $2.5 million, or $3.5 million, stated alone without qualification.
killed.why: The two primary sources disagree ($2.5M on xprize.org and in Dryad's release, $3.5M in the PR Newswire release). Either figure alone misleads. Use the reconciled wording in S1-C04 and S1-C05.
It appears on no page. It is arithmetic (1.2M + 1M). It can only appear as an explicit sum of two separately sourced awards.

killed.claim: Anduril's Ghost-X aircraft delivered fire retardant balls during the Alaska test.
killed.why: The fetch returned it as paraphrase outside quotation marks, so the verbatim text could not be confirmed.

killed.claim: Any Alaska Division of Forestry and Fire Protection, Alaska Fire Service or BLM role in the finals.
killed.why: Not stated on any fetched page. The only Alaska institutions named are UAF and ACUASI.

killed.claim: The size of the test fires, their ignition method, and the weather on test days at Nenana.
killed.why: Not stated on any fetched page. The pages only say 'controlled incipient stage wildfires' and describe generic Interior conditions.

killed.claim: Independent Alaska newsroom or trade coverage of the September 23rd awards.
killed.why: None found. UAF News has no XPRIZE item, DroneLife has only a May 18th student piece, and the search engines were blocked. Story 1 rests on XPRIZE and Dryad primaries.

killed.claim: Treg Taylor and Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins spoke at a September 8th forum.
killed.why: The forum date appeared in only one paraphrasing fetch and was not reproduced verbatim.
